topic_summary: Analysis of Quran 9:5 ('Sword Verse') as a contested interpretive kernel. The verse commands treatment of polytheists after sacred months expire. Two principal readings emit structurally different constraints: an abrogating-universal reading authorizing offensive jihad until global submission, and a contextual-defensive reading limiting application to specific 7th-century treaty violations while prioritizing peaceful coexistence.

key_entities: Quran 9:5 (Sword Verse text commanding treatment of polytheists)
Classical abrogation theory (naskh doctrine claiming later verses supersede earlier)
7th-century Medinan treaty context (Peace of Hudaybiyyah; subsequent violations)
Modernist tafsir tradition (contextual hermeneutic emphasizing historical specificity)
Revivalist jihadist movements (groups invoking universal applicability for armed expansion)
Peaceful Quranic verses (e.g., 2:256 'no compulsion in religion'; 60:8 justice to peaceful non-Muslims)
key_tensions: Temporal scope: universal command vs historically-bounded directive (abrogating vs contextual readings)
Legitimate violence authority: standing authorization vs defensive contingency (offensive vs defensive jihad doctrines)
key_mechanisms: Abrogation doctrine (naskh): textual mechanism declaring later-revealed verses supersede earlier contradictory ones
Treaty violation recognition: interpretive mechanism determining when peace obligations no longer bind
key_absences: Absence of unified Sunni ijma (consensus) on verse's scope despite centrality to jurisprudence
Absence of direct Quranic meta-commentary on verse 9:5's relationship to peaceful verses
Absence of treatment of Shiite jurisprudential tradition (analysis confined to Sunni interpretive spectrum)

axiom_contradictions.basis: Accepting that later revelation categorically supersedes earlier peaceful commands (abrogation axiom) requires rejecting the axiom that Quranic peaceful verses remain operative law. No single framework holds both 'verse 9:5 abrogates 2:256' and 'verse 2:256 remains binding' as true simultaneously.

Accepting that Quranic text is eternal divine command requiring literal obedience (classical uṣūl axiom) requires rejecting that historical context renders directives non-binding (progressive historicist axiom). No coherent framework holds both textual eternalism and historical obsolescence.

Accepting that verse 9:5 remains legally operative when contextual conditions obtain (treaty violation) requires rejecting that the verse has exited legal force entirely. A framework cannot simultaneously bind actors to conditional treaty-based warfare and declare the directive categorically non-binding.

omegas.description: Analysis confined to Sunni interpretive spectrum. Shiite jurisprudence (Ja'fari fiqh) has distinct abrogation doctrine and imamological interpretive authority. Structural delta unknown; may constitute fourth reading with different authority grounding.

Lack of unified Sunni consensus (ijma) on verse scope suggests interpretive instability is structural feature rather than resolvable dispute. If no ijma is possible, the kernel may be deliberately polysemous (Interpretive Capture pattern confirmed).

Modern nation-states instrumentalize both readings (abrogating for external enemies, contextual for internal pluralism). This dual deployment may constitute fifth reading: Pragmatic Instrumentalism, where verse scope flexes with state interest rather than fixed hermeneutic commitment.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) — state actors not cleanly aligned with either reading

omegas.description: Quran itself contains no explicit meta-verse declaring 9:5's relationship to peaceful verses. Abrogation doctrine is extra-Quranic (hadith-derived). If naskh doctrine is itself contested, the kernel's contested status may be artifact of later jurisprudential layer rather than inherent scriptural ambiguity.
